gateway.text:
The key difference is **who does the recognizing**.

- **Personalized cancer vaccine:** the vaccine supplies cancer-related material or instructions. It does not usually give immune cells a new receptor. Instead, it tries to **teach or expand the patient’s T cells** to recognize tumor fragments. A mutation is only a candidate target: it must be present, expressed, processed into a peptide, and displayed by HLA—the cell’s “display holder.” The T-cell receptor then recognizes the **peptide–HLA pair** [vaccine overview](/education/guides/personalized-cancer-vaccine/index/#the-big-ideas).

- **Engineered cell therapy:** the treatment gives T cells or other immune cells a selected receptor. Those cells are designed to recognize a defined target directly. A **CAR** usually recognizes an accessible molecule on the tumor-cell surface; an engineered **TCR** recognizes a peptide–HLA complex. Target selection therefore asks which cells carry the target, whether the receptor can physically reach it, and whether healthy tissues also carry it [target selection](/education/guides/engineered-cell-therapy/02-choosing-a-target/#specify-the-target-at-the-level-the-receptor-reads).

**Analogy:** a vaccine teaches the security team what to look for; engineered cells arrive with a chosen scanner already installed.

Would you like a simple side-by-side example using a mutation-derived peptide versus a surface protein?
